name: Symplectic tracking of beams
summary: Long-term tracking in storage rings uses symplectic maps and integrators so that dynamic-aperture studies over 10^5–10^7 turns have no artificial damping or growth, as in long-term celestial mechanics.

name: Scaling laws in cell and membrane mechanics
summary: Scaling sets cell-scale physics. Swimming bacteria have Re ~ 10^-4, so inertia is irrelevant and reciprocal strokes fail (Purcell's scallop theorem). The membrane length √(κ/σ), tens to hundreds of nm, separates bending-dominated from tension-dominated regimes and sets tether radii.

name: Kelvin's circulation theorem from relabelling symmetry
summary: Ideal barotropic flow follows from Hamilton's principle written in fluid-particle labels. The action is invariant under mass-preserving relabelling of parcels, and Noether's theorem for this infinite-dimensional symmetry gives Kelvin's circulation theorem and the conservation of potential vorticity.
breaks: Viscosity and non-conservative forcing destroy the variational structure and with it the theorem.

name: Elastic P, S and Rayleigh waves
summary: Navier's equations of linear elasticity admit compressional (P) and shear (S) waves, with speeds set by the Lamé moduli, plus Rayleigh surface waves at ≈0.92 c_S for Poisson ratio 0.25. Acoustics in solids is linear elastodynamics, the basis of seismology and ultrasonic testing.

name: Convection as the testbed for routes to chaos
summary: Rayleigh–Bénard convection begins at Ra_c≈1708 (infinite layer, rigid plates) through a symmetry-breaking pitchfork of the conducting state. In small-aspect-ratio cells, Libchaber and Maurer observed period-doubling cascades whose ratios approached Feigenbaum's δ, and other cells showed quasiperiodic and intermittent routes. These experiments tested bifurcation universality in a real fluid.

name: Lorenz equations: a truncated Rayleigh–Bénard model
summary: Lorenz's three ODEs are a three-mode Galerkin truncation (after Saltzman) of 2D Boussinesq convection: x is the roll amplitude, y and z are temperature modes, ρ=Ra/Ra_c and σ is the Prandtl number. The strange attractor of this truncation launched modern chaos theory.
breaks: Real convection near ρ≈28 is three-dimensional and far from three-mode; the equations are exact only for analogues such as the chaotic waterwheel and the single-mode laser.

name: Convection rolls as the paradigm of pattern formation
summary: Rayleigh–Bénard convection above Ra_c≈1708 is the archetypal stationary pattern-forming instability (rolls, hexagons, Eckhaus and zigzag instabilities, spiral-defect chaos); near onset the roll envelope obeys the Ginzburg–Landau (Newell–Whitehead–Segel) amplitude equation, also derivable from the Swift–Hohenberg model.

name: Bertrand's theorem and the Kepler–oscillator duality
summary: Bertrand's theorem: among central potentials, only 1/r and r² make every bounded orbit close. The two are dual. The conformal map z=w² with a time reparametrization (Bohlin, Levi-Civita; Kustaanheimo–Stiefel in 3D) sends centred oscillator ellipses to focal Kepler ellipses and exchanges the roles of energy and coupling constant.

name: Poincaré's three-body homoclinic tangle
summary: While correcting his 1889–90 prize memoir on the restricted three-body problem, Poincaré found that the stable and unstable manifolds of periodic orbits intersect transversally and fold into homoclinic tangles, the first recognition of deterministic chaos. Modern integrations show the inner Solar System is chaotic, with a Lyapunov time of ~5 Myr (Laskar).

name: Planetary stability: surviving tori and resonances
summary: KAM theory grew out of the perturbed Kepler problem. For small planetary masses most quasi-periodic orbits survive as invariant tori (Arnold's planetary theorem), while mean-motion and secular resonances carve out chaotic zones such as the Kirkwood gap at the 3:1 resonance with Jupiter. Hénon and Heiles showed that a third integral breaks down for galactic orbits.

name: Driven nonlinear oscillators: bifurcations to chaos
summary: The Mathieu instability tongues are bifurcations of the oscillator's rest state. The driven Duffing oscillator shows saddle-node (jump) bifurcations and hysteresis in its response curve. The driven damped pendulum and Duffing oscillator reach chaos through period-doubling cascades with Feigenbaum's universal ratio δ≈4.669.

name: Linear canonical transforms in Fresnel optics
summary: Paraxial propagation through any ABCD system is the Collins integral, which is the wave (metaplectic) representation of the linear canonical transformation given by the symplectic ray matrix. Free space acts as a Fresnel transform and a thin lens as a quadratic phase. A graded-index medium, whose ray Hamiltonian is a harmonic oscillator, performs a fractional Fourier transform that becomes the full Fourier transform after a quarter period.
breaks: The correspondence is exact only in the paraxial limit. Aberrations make the ray map nonlinear, and the wave propagator then stops being a simple metaplectic integral.

name: Eikonal equation is the Hamilton–Jacobi equation
summary: The eikonal equation |∇S|²=n² is the stationary Hamilton–Jacobi equation: wavefronts S=const are level sets of Hamilton's characteristic function, and rays are its characteristics. Both sides become multivalued at caustics, where diffraction or Maslov phases enter. Hamilton developed the method for optics and carried it to dynamics in 1834–35, and Schrödinger completed the optico-mechanical analogy into wave mechanics.

breaks: Both solutions become multivalued at caustics and focal points. There geometric optics fails, and diffraction (or Maslov phases, in semiclassics) must be added.

name: Charged-particle Lagrangian and minimal coupling
summary: The Lorentz force follows from Lagrange's equations with the velocity-dependent potential U=q(φ−v·A), and the canonical momentum p=mv+qA differs from the kinetic momentum. A gauge transformation adds q dχ/dt to L and leaves the motion unchanged. Classically only the fields act on the particle; the same minimal coupling underlies the quantum Aharonov–Bohm phase q∮A·dl/ħ.
map: L=\tfrac12mv^2-q\phi+q\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf A;\ \mathbf p=m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A;\ H=\frac{(\mathbf p-q\mathbf A)^2}{2m}+q\phi;\ L\to L+q\frac{d\chi}{dt}
breaks: Classically only the fields matter. That the potentials themselves have physical effects (the Aharonov–Bohm effect) appears only in quantum mechanics.

name: Fermat's principle and the principle of least action
summary: Light rays make the optical path stationary in the same way that mechanical trajectories make the action stationary. In Maupertuis' form δ∫p ds=0, ray optics maps onto mechanics with the refractive index in the role of momentum, so Snell's law becomes conservation of momentum parallel to the interface.
breaks: The map holds at fixed energy, which means a single frequency. The particle's speed is proportional to n, while light's phase velocity is c/n. Hamilton and de Broglie resolved this mismatch by distinguishing phase velocity from group velocity.

name: Vortex Biot–Savart law: vorticity as current
summary: An incompressible velocity field obeys ∇·u=0 and ∇×u=ω, the same equations as B with source μ0J. Vortex lines therefore induce velocity by the Biot–Savart law: a line vortex acts like a straight wire and a vortex ring like a current loop. Maxwell's 1861 molecular-vortex model ran the analogy the other way, to picture magnetic fields.
map: \mathbf u=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\boldsymbol\omega'\times\mathbf R}{R^3}dV'\ \leftrightarrow\ \mathbf B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{\mathbf J'\times\mathbf R}{R^3}dV',\ \mathbf R=\mathbf r-\mathbf r'
breaks: Vorticity is carried along and stretched by the velocity it induces (Helmholtz's laws), so vortex dynamics is nonlinear, whereas currents are prescribed. Parallel vortices of the same sign orbit each other instead of attracting the way parallel currents do.

name: Atmospheric seeing: Kolmogorov turbulence limits coherence
summary: Kolmogorov scaling of temperature fluctuations makes the refractive-index structure function grow as r^(2/3), so starlight picks up a phase structure function proportional to (r/r0)^(5/3). The Fried parameter r0 sets the spatial coherence length and limits telescope resolution to about λ/r0. The result is speckle, which motivated speckle interferometry and adaptive optics.
breaks: Real atmospheric turbulence has finite outer and inner scales and is intermittent, so the 5/3 law fails at the largest and smallest separations.

name: Larmor radiation and the collapse of classical atoms
summary: An electron on a classical Kepler orbit around a nucleus radiates at the Larmor rate and spirals inward within about 10⁻¹¹ s. This failure of Rutherford's planetary atom motivated Bohr's stationary orbits. The same radiative decay of orbits shapes cyclotron and synchrotron motion.
breaks: In quantum mechanics there is no continuous inspiral. Stationary states replace it, and radiation occurs only in transitions at discrete frequencies.

name: Larmor's theorem: Coriolis force mimics a magnetic field
summary: In a frame rotating at Ω, the Coriolis force 2m v×Ω has the same form as the magnetic force q v×B. Rotating at Ω=−qB/2m therefore removes a weak uniform field to first order, which explains the Larmor precession of orbits and atomic diamagnetism. Conversely, rotating neutral systems can simulate magnetic fields.
breaks: The equivalence holds only to first order. The rotating frame adds a centrifugal force of order Ω² with no magnetic counterpart, which must be small or cancelled by a trap.

name: Optical solitons from the integrable NLS equation
summary: A pulse envelope in a Kerr fibre with anomalous dispersion obeys the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which inverse scattering solves exactly. Self-phase modulation balances group-velocity dispersion, and the fundamental sech soliton (N=1) and the higher-order breathers are the same objects found in deep-water wave groups.
breaks: Real fibres add loss, the Raman self-frequency shift and higher-order dispersion, all of which break integrability. Solitons then shed dispersive waves and undergo fission, which is what drives supercontinuum generation.

name: Cavity modes and LC lines as mechanical oscillators
summary: Each normal mode of a resonant cavity obeys a damped driven oscillator equation, with the quality factor Q=ω0/Δω defined exactly as for a mechanical resonator. A lumped LC transmission line is a mass–spring chain (L↔m, 1/C↔k): it has the same discrete-lattice dispersion and cutoff, and its continuum limit is the same wave equation.
map: \ddot a+\frac{\omega_0}{Q}\dot a+\omega_0^2a=f(t);\ L\leftrightarrow m,\ C^{-1}\leftrightarrow k,\ R\leftrightarrow b;\ \omega(k)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{LC}}\left|\sin\frac{ka}{2}\right|
breaks: The analogy holds mode by mode, but not for the field's spatial structure. Cavity modes carry polarization and vector boundary conditions, and their density grows as ω², which a scalar chain does not reproduce.

name: Radiation reaction as oscillator damping
summary: A charged oscillator loses energy at the Larmor rate. For near-harmonic motion the Abraham–Lorentz force mτ0 d³x/dt³ reduces to a damping rate γ=ω0²τ0. This gives the classical natural linewidth Δλ=(4π/3)re≈1.2×10⁻¹⁴ m, independent of frequency.
breaks: Taken exactly, the third-order Abraham–Lorentz equation has runaway solutions and preacceleration, so it is used only perturbatively (the Landau–Lifshitz form). For atoms, quantum linewidths replace the classical value.

name: Brillouin scattering couples light to sound
summary: Light Bragg-reflects off an acoustic wave and is Doppler-shifted by the sound frequency. At high intensity, electrostriction drives the acoustic wave itself, giving stimulated Brillouin scattering. For narrow-linewidth light this is the lowest-threshold fibre nonlinearity, with a shift of about 11 GHz in silica at 1550 nm, and it is used in Brillouin lasers, slow light and distributed strain sensing.

name: Kapitza effective potential is the ponderomotive energy
summary: Averaging motion in a rapidly oscillating force F0 cos ωt gives Kapitza's effective potential F0²/4mω². For an electron in a laser field this is the ponderomotive energy Up. It sets the strong-field scales of attosecond physics, including the high-harmonic cutoff Ip+3.17Up, and it pushes electrons out of intense foci.
breaks: The averaging requires the field to vary slowly in space over one quiver excursion. At relativistic intensities (a0≳1), magnetic forces and the relativistic mass increase modify Up.

name: Sagnac interferometers as optical gyroscopes
summary: Beams sent both ways around a loop rotating at Ω pick up a phase difference proportional to the enclosed area, which gives an absolute measurement of rotation. Ring-laser and fibre-optic gyroscopes built on this effect have largely replaced spinning-rotor gyroscopes in inertial navigation. Large ring lasers resolve Earth's rotation.
breaks: The optical device has no angular momentum. It senses rotation through the light travel time in the rotating frame, not through gyroscopic rigidity, so it shows no precession or nutation and needs no spin-up.

name: Navier–Stokes from Boltzmann (Chapman–Enskog)
summary: Expanding the Boltzmann equation in the Knudsen number (Chapman–Enskog) gives the Euler equations at zeroth order and Navier–Stokes at first order, with the viscosity and heat conductivity computed from the cross-section. The lattice Boltzmann method runs this in reverse: it simulates flows using a discretized BGK collision operator.
breaks: Valid only for Kn≪1. Rarefied flows need the kinetic description, and higher-order (Burnett) corrections are ill-behaved.

name: Amplitude equations as time-dependent Landau theory
summary: Near the onset of Rayleigh–Bénard convection (Ra_c ≈ 1708 for rigid plates), the roll amplitude obeys the Newell–Whitehead–Segel (real Ginzburg–Landau) equation, which has the form of time-dependent Landau theory. Supercritical onset gives A ∝ ε^{1/2}, a coherence length ∝ ε^{-1/2} and a relaxation time ∝ ε^{-1}.
breaks: Pattern-forming systems are driven and usually non-variational (complex Ginzburg–Landau has no free energy). Thermal fluctuations matter only extremely close to onset, where they make the transition weakly first order (Swift–Hohenberg), and the broken symmetry is a spatial pattern with wavenumber selection.

name: Stokes drag sets Brownian diffusion (Stokes–Einstein)
summary: The low-Reynolds-number drag 6πηa on a sphere is the friction coefficient in the overdamped Langevin equation, and Einstein's relation turns it into D = k_BT/6πηa. For micron colloids inertia relaxes in about 0.1 µs. Hydrodynamic memory (Basset force) matters below about a²/ν, and Stokes–Einstein breaks down for molecular solutes and supercooled liquids.
breaks: At times of order a²/ν, unsteady-Stokes hydrodynamic memory (Basset force, t^{-3/2} velocity tails) makes the noise coloured. This was observed by Franosch et al. (2011).

name: Onset of wall-bounded turbulence as directed percolation
summary: Near the onset of sustained wall-bounded turbulence, turbulent patches decay and split like active sites in an absorbing-state transition, with laminar flow absorbing (Pomeau's conjecture). In 2016, Couette (Lemoult et al.) and channel (Sano–Tamai) experiments measured 1+1 and 2+1 DP exponents. In pipe flow, puff decay balances splitting at Re ≈ 2040.

name: Virial theorem and negative heat capacity
summary: For bound 1/r systems the virial theorem gives E = −⟨K⟩, so a star or star cluster that loses energy heats up (C < 0). Such states exist in the microcanonical ensemble but not in the canonical one. This is the textbook case of ensemble inequivalence for long-range interactions and the root of the gravothermal catastrophe.

name: Chaotic diffusion in the standard map
summary: Once the last KAM barrier breaks (K ≈ 0.9716), momentum in the Chirikov standard map spreads without bound, so a deterministic Hamiltonian map behaves like a Fokker–Planck process. Just above K_c, leaky cantori make diffusion slow (D ∝ (K−K_c)^3). For K≫1 it approaches the quasilinear rate K²/2, with oscillatory corrections. Accelerator modes and stickiness near islands make transport anomalous.

name: Phonons: quantized normal modes and heat capacity
summary: Normal-mode analysis turns a harmonic crystal into independent oscillators. Quantized, these become a Bose gas of phonons with zero chemical potential, and the Planck-weighted mode sum gives the Einstein and Debye heat capacities (C ∝ T³ at low T) and the classical Dulong–Petit limit 3Nk_B from equipartition.

name: Sound propagation and absorption from kinetic theory
summary: The adiabatic sound speed and the classical Stokes–Kirchhoff absorption both follow from the hydrodynamic limit of the Boltzmann equation, with attenuation set by viscosity and thermal conduction. When ωτ ~ 1, at high frequency or in a rarefied gas, hydrodynamic acoustics breaks down and BGK-type kinetic models describe the sound instead.

name: Bohmian mechanics as quantum Hamilton–Jacobi theory
summary: With ψ=R e^{iS/ħ}, the Schrödinger equation is exactly a Hamilton–Jacobi equation plus Bohm's quantum potential Q (Madelung 1927, Bohm 1952). De Broglie–Bohm theory has particles move along v=∇S/m, the characteristics of this equation, which gives a deterministic hidden-variable interpretation.
breaks: For many particles Q is nonlocal in configuration space and does not weaken as |ψ| shrinks. The motion is first-order, so initial momenta are not free. The mathematics is exact, but the interpretation is contested.

name: WKB: Schrödinger reduces to Hamilton–Jacobi
summary: Writing ψ=A e^{iS/ħ} turns the Schrödinger equation into the Hamilton–Jacobi equation at leading order, plus a continuity equation for A. Quantizing the action variables J=∮p dq gives the Bohr–Sommerfeld and EBK rules. Ehrenfest argued that action variables were the right quantities to quantize because they are adiabatic invariants.
breaks: It breaks down at turning points and caustics, where A diverges (Airy matching and the Maslov 1/2 repair this), and wherever the de Broglie wavelength changes quickly.

name: Hamilton's principal function as the semiclassical phase
summary: In the stationary-phase evaluation of the path integral, the phase is Hamilton's principal function S(x_b,x_a,t), which generates the classical time-evolution map. The prefactor is its mixed second derivative (the Van Vleck–Gutzwiller propagator), and caustics of the classical family add Maslov phases.
breaks: It fails near caustics and beyond the Ehrenfest time, where classical paths proliferate (chaos). It also fails where no real classical path exists: tunnelling needs complex or Euclidean paths.

name: Phase-space QM: Liouville flow to Wigner–Moyal
summary: The Wigner function is a quasi-probability on classical phase space that evolves by the Liouville equation with the Poisson bracket replaced by the Moyal bracket. Quantum optics describes light with Wigner, Husimi-Q and Glauber–Sudarshan-P distributions; Wigner negativity or a singular P function marks a nonclassical state.
map: \partial_tW=\{H,W\}_{\star}=\{H,W\}+O(\hbar^2\,\partial^3H\,\partial^3W);\ \ W\ \text{follows the classical flow exactly if}\ H\ \text{is quadratic}
breaks: W can be negative, so it is not a probability. Moyal corrections at O(ħ²) appear for anharmonic Hamiltonians, so classical Liouville flow is exact only for quadratic H (linear optics).

name: Circuit quantization from the node-flux Lagrangian
summary: Superconducting circuits are quantized by writing a Lagrangian in node fluxes, with capacitive energy as kinetic energy and inductive and Josephson energy as potential energy. A Legendre transform makes the charges the conjugate momenta, and one then imposes [Φ,Q]=iħ. Kirchhoff loops and flux quantization act as holonomic constraints.
breaks: Dissipative and non-Lagrangian elements (resistors, nonreciprocal gyrators) need a bath or an extended treatment. Offset charges and compact phase variables need care.

name: Madelung: condensates as inviscid, irrotational fluids
summary: With ψ=√n e^{iθ}, the Gross–Pitaevskii equation becomes the continuity and Euler equations of an inviscid, irrotational fluid with velocity v=ħ∇θ/m, plus a quantum-pressure term. Kelvin's circulation theorem becomes the topological quantization of circulation around vortex lines, and the Landau criterion sets the critical velocity for dissipation.
map: \mathbf v=\tfrac{\hbar}{m}\nabla\theta;\ \ m\partial_t\mathbf v=-\nabla\big(\tfrac12mv^2+V+gn+Q\big);\ \ \oint\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf l=\tfrac{h}{m}\ell,\ \ell\in\mathbb Z
breaks: The fluid picture fails inside vortex cores and below the healing length ξ, where quantum pressure dominates. At finite temperature a normal component adds viscosity (the two-fluid model).

name: Atom interferometers as gravimeters and Sagnac gyroscopes
summary: Light-pulse atom interferometers turn the classical kinematics of free fall and rotating frames into matter-wave phases. The gravity phase k_eff g T² underlies atomic gravimeters, and the Sagnac phase from Earth's rotation makes atom gyroscopes; when rotation is not the target, the Coriolis terms must be compensated.
breaks: For equal area, the matter-wave Sagnac phase exceeds the optical one by mc²/ħω ~ 10^10, but atom interferometers enclose far smaller areas.
